draft.title: Australian Dietary Guidelines
card: The Australian Dietary Guidelines are advice from the Australian Government on what to eat for good health. They are based on research and are written for the general population.
There are five guidelines. The first is to be physically active and eat enough food to keep a healthy body weight. The second is to enjoy a wide range of nutritious foods from the five food groups.
The third is to limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and added sugars, and to limit alcohol. The fourth is to encourage, support and promote breastfeeding.
The fifth is to care for your food: prepare and store it safely. The guidelines are advice for healthy eating, not laws.
draft.remember: The guidelines advise eating a variety of nutritious foods and limiting saturated fat, added salt, added sugars and alcohol.

a.q: Which choice follows the Australian Dietary Guidelines?
opts: Eating a wide range of foods from the five food groups
Cutting out all foods from one food group to lose weight
Eating the same few foods each day so meals stay simple
Adding extra salt to meals to make them tastier
a.why: The guidelines advise enjoying a wide range of nutritious foods from the five food groups. Cutting out a whole food group goes against this, even if the aim is weight loss.
a.clue: Think about the word range in the guidelines.

b.q: Tom, 16, has chips, a sausage roll and a sugary drink for lunch most days. Which guideline is he most clearly not following?
opts: Limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and sugars
Care for your food by storing it safely
Encourage, support and promote breastfeeding
Enjoy a wide range of foods from the five food groups
b.why: Chips, sausage rolls and sugary drinks are usually high in saturated fat, added salt or added sugars, so the limiting guideline fits best. Variety is also lacking, but the foods named are the clearest sign of a lack of limits.
b.clue: Look at what the foods in his lunch are high in.

a.best: Eating a wide range of foods from the five food groups

b.best: Limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and sugars
also_right: Enjoy a wide range of foods from the five food groups

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about the word range in the guidelines' gives the answer away, because only the right option contains the word 'range'. A student can match the word without knowing the guideline.

Guideline 1 is paraphrased as 'eat enough food to keep a healthy body weight'. The actual guideline is to choose amounts of nutritious food and drinks to meet your energy needs. 'Eat enough' suggests a minimum and could mislead students, since the main concern is usually not eating more than you need.

check.summary: The facts on the five guidelines are correct, and both questions have a clear best answer, though variety in (b) is also defensible, as the why admits. The clue for (a) gives the answer away by naming 'range', and the card's wording of guideline 1 ('eat enough') slightly misrepresents its meaning.

proposal.title: The Australian Dietary Guidelines
card: The Australian Dietary Guidelines are advice from the National Health and Medical Research Council, an Australian Government agency, on eating for good health. They are based on research and written for the general population.

Guideline 1: be physically active and choose amounts of nutritious food and drinks to meet your energy needs, to reach and keep a healthy weight. Guideline 2: enjoy a wide variety of nutritious foods from the five food groups every day, and drink plenty of water.
Guideline 3: limit foods and drinks with saturated fat, added salt and added sugars, and limit alcohol. Guideline 4: encourage, support and promote breastfeeding.
Guideline 5: care for your food by preparing and storing it safely. The guidelines are advice for healthy eating, not laws.
proposal.remember: Match food to energy needs, eat a variety, limit the less healthy extras, support breastfeeding and keep food safe.

a.q: Which choice follows the Australian Dietary Guidelines?
opts: Drinking water instead of a daily soft drink
Cutting out a whole food group to lose weight
Adding salt to vegetables so they taste better
Skipping exercise but eating smaller meals
a.why: Swapping soft drink for water cuts added sugars and follows the advice to drink plenty of water. Eating smaller meals while skipping exercise may seem healthy, but guideline 1 asks people to be physically active as well as matching food to energy needs.
a.clue: Check each choice against all five guidelines, not just one.

b.q: Jack cooks rice and vegetables on Sunday night. He leaves the leftovers on the bench until Monday evening, then eats them. Which guideline does this go against?
opts: Care for your food: prepare and store it safely
Limit saturated fat, added salt and added sugars
Enjoy a wide variety of foods from the five food groups
Choose amounts of food and drink to meet energy needs
b.why: Leaving cooked food on the bench for a day lets bacteria grow, so Jack is not storing his food safely. Rice and vegetables are not high in saturated fat, added salt or added sugars, so the limiting guideline does not fit.
b.clue: The problem is not what he ate, but where it spent the day.

a.best: Drinking water instead of a daily soft drink

b.best: Care for your food: prepare and store it safely
